headline: Green tribunal imposes Rs 13 lakh on Arkavathi Dyes for effluent discharge
body:
NASHIK: The National Green Tribunal's Western Zone bench at Pune has directed Arkavathi Dyes & Pigments Ltd to pay environmental compensation of Rs 13 lakh for release of untreated effluent into a nearby drain at its Nashik Chemical Complex in Nashik, Maharashtra, according to an order dated 26 July 2019. The matter was registered as O.A. No. 514/2019 (WZ).

In its order, the bench applied the polluter pays principle and asked the Maharashtra Pollution Control Board to monitor compliance and report back to the tribunal. The tribunal said that the amount is meant to restore the environment and is not a substitute for any prosecution that the board may initiate under the Water and Air Acts.

Online monitoring data on the public portal show 2 recorded exceedances at the facility in the twelve months before the order. Company filings indicate that Arkavathi Dyes has since paid the amount.

The company's chief sustainability officer said that the company is studying the order and remains committed to compliance with all applicable norms. The Nashik Chemical Complex has a capacity of 850,000 tpa and operates under consent number MPCB/CTO/2015/82027.

headline: BRSR Core assurance: the glide path for India's listed companies
body:
SEBI's glide path for assurance on BRSR Core indicators brings the largest listed companies into a regime where nine ESG attributes are verified by an independent provider, starting with limited assurance and moving towards reasonable assurance.

Assurance providers say that demand has outstripped supply of qualified practitioners, particularly for greenhouse gas verification at industrial sites, and that fees have risen.

Investors have welcomed the move but note that the scope and conclusion of each assurance statement differ, and that a qualified conclusion or a narrow scope tells a different story from an unmodified one.

Companies that have moved early to reasonable assurance argue that it forces better controls on data, while others say that the cost and effort are material for mid-sized firms.

Practitioners said that the most common qualifications relate to estimated water withdrawal, default emission factors for fugitive emissions and incomplete contractor safety data, which are areas where systems are still maturing.

Regulators have indicated that they will review the first full cycle of assured filings before deciding on the next phase of the glide path.

headline: BRSR Core assurance: the glide path for India's listed companies
body:
SEBI's glide path for assurance on BRSR Core indicators brings the largest listed companies into a regime where nine ESG attributes are verified by an independent provider, starting with limited assurance and moving towards reasonable assurance.

Assurance providers say that demand has outstripped supply of qualified practitioners, particularly for greenhouse gas verification at industrial sites, and that fees have risen.

Investors have welcomed the move but note that the scope and conclusion of each assurance statement differ, and that a qualified conclusion or a narrow scope tells a different story from an unmodified one.

Companies that have moved early to reasonable assurance argue that it forces better controls on data, while others say that the cost and effort are material for mid-sized firms.

Practitioners said that the most common qualifications relate to estimated water withdrawal, default emission factors for fugitive emissions and incomplete contractor safety data, which are areas where systems are still maturing.

Regulators have indicated that they will review the first full cycle of assured filings before deciding on the next phase of the glide path.

Rating agencies said that they now routinely compare company filings with regulatory orders and satellite data before assigning ESG scores.

Companies in heavy industry have been asked by lenders and customers to disclose facility-level data, and many have started to publish site-wise emissions and water use alongside their annual reports.

Environmental lawyers said that the quality of data is now a bigger issue than its availability, since regulators, investors and communities increasingly compare several sources before forming a view on a company.

Industry associations said that compliance costs have risen across sectors, but argued that predictable rules and clear timelines are more important to investment decisions than the level of any single norm.

Sustainability consultants said that the gap between voluntary targets and filed numbers is where most disputes arise, and recommended that companies reconcile their communications with their regulatory filings every year.

SEBI's Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report framework requires the top listed companies to disclose a core set of indicators and, in phases, to obtain external assurance on them, which has made company-level numbers easier to compare.

Investors and rating agencies have begun to cross-check company disclosures against regulatory orders, satellite data and certificate registries, rather than relying on sustainability reports alone.

Analysts caution that headline sustainability claims are best read alongside the filed numbers, since the choice of baseline year and the use of intensity rather than absolute figures can change the picture considerably.

BALLARI: The Central Pollution Control Board has directed Apatani Green Power Ltd to pay environmental compensation of Rs 11 lakh for stack emission exceedances recorded by the online monitoring system at its Ballari Biomass Power Plant in Ballari, Karnataka. The order is dated 2 February 2024 and carries the reference CPCB/IPC-II/KA/2024/574.

An official familiar with the matter said that the amount was calculated on the basis of the unit's scale and the period of the violation, in line with the compensation formula adopted by the regulator. The company has been given a fixed period to deposit the sum and to file a compliance report.

Company filings indicate that Apatani Green has since paid the amount. The company's head of environment, health and safety said that the company has taken corrective steps at the site.

Located in Ballari, the Ballari Biomass Power Plant has a capacity of 34 MW. The company's other facilities are in Karnataka.

Operators of coal-fired plants face tighter norms on particulate matter, sulphur dioxide and fly ash utilisation, while developers of solar and wind parks face land, transmission and offtake challenges.

In its BRSR for FY2022-23, Apatani Green reported Scope 1 emissions of 16,448 tCO2e, Scope 2 emissions of 21,708 tCO2e and a GHG intensity of 4.5 tCO2e per Rs crore of turnover, with 63.6% of its electricity from renewable sources. The disclosure was not externally assured.

Apatani Green Power Ltd is a power generation company headquartered in Bengaluru, Karnataka. It reported turnover of Rs 8,392 crore in FY2022-23 and operates 2 facilities across Karnataka. Its shares trade under the listing NSE: APATAPWR.

headline: Mining emission league table, FY2022-23: who is cleanest per rupee
body:
An analysis of BRSR filings for FY2022-23 across 15 mining companies shows a wide spread in greenhouse gas intensity, measured as Scope 1 plus Scope 2 emissions per Rs crore of turnover. The median was 127.4 tCO2e per Rs crore.

The lowest intensities were reported by Parvati Coal & Minerals Ltd (62.6 tCO2e per Rs crore), Kangra Minerals Ltd (64.2 tCO2e per Rs crore) and Ghaghara Manganese & Minerals Ltd (68.5 tCO2e per Rs crore).

At the other end, the highest intensities were reported by Wainganga Minerals Ltd (173.3 tCO2e per Rs crore), Pinaka Mining Industries Ltd (158.3 tCO2e per Rs crore) and Varuna Ores Ltd (152.9 tCO2e per Rs crore). The top of the range is 2.8 times the bottom.

The median in the previous year was 131.4 tCO2e per Rs crore, so the sector median moved by -3.0% year on year. Of the 15 filings, 7 carried some form of external assurance.

Analysts cautioned that product mix, fuel mix and the share of captive power explain much of the difference, and that intensity comparisons are most meaningful within narrow sub-segments.

They added that intensity can improve while absolute emissions rise, and that investors should read both figures together with the assurance level of each filing.

Companies in heavy industry have been asked by lenders and customers to disclose facility-level data, and many have started to publish site-wise emissions and water use alongside their annual reports.

headline: Green tribunal imposes Rs 6.23 crore on Khasi Forgings for stack emissions
body:

The matter was registered as O.A. No. 482/2024 (PB).

The tribunal said that the amount is meant to restore the environment and is not a substitute for any prosecution that the board may initiate under the Water and Air Acts.

Online monitoring data on the public portal show 3 recorded exceedances at the facility in the twelve months before the order. Khasi Forgings has challenged the order in appeal, and the matter is pending.

A company spokesperson said that the company is studying the order and remains committed to compliance with all applicable norms. The Meerut Foundry has a capacity of 76,000 tpa castings and operates under consent number UPPCB/CTO/2018/33413.

headline: Forest clearances and the new role of satellite alerts
body:
Mining and industrial lease holders are finding that satellite-based forest-loss alerts are being used by communities, researchers and regulators to question activity near their sites.

Alert systems detect loss of tree cover at a fine resolution and publish it within days, but they do not attribute responsibility, and field verification remains essential.

Forest officials said that they have begun to cross-check alerts against clearance maps, while companies say that they need clear protocols on how alerts will be treated.

Researchers cautioned against reading too much into single alerts, but said that clusters near a lease over a year deserve scrutiny.

Companies with zero-deforestation commitments said that they are adding satellite monitoring to their own reporting, so that they can respond before a third party raises a question.

Legal experts said that a satellite alert is not proof of a violation, but that a pattern of alerts within a lease buffer could shift the burden of explanation onto the operator.

The ministry is expected to consult industry before notifying the final rules, and stakeholders have been asked to submit comments.

Companies in heavy industry have been asked by lenders and customers to disclose facility-level data, and many have started to publish site-wise emissions and water use alongside their annual reports.

Environmental lawyers said that the quality of data is now a bigger issue than its availability, since regulators, investors and communities increasingly compare several sources before forming a view on a company.

Industry associations said that compliance costs have risen across sectors, but argued that predictable rules and clear timelines are more important to investment decisions than the level of any single norm.

Sustainability consultants said that the gap between voluntary targets and filed numbers is where most disputes arise, and recommended that companies reconcile their communications with their regulatory filings every year.

SEBI's Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report framework requires the top listed companies to disclose a core set of indicators and, in phases, to obtain external assurance on them, which has made company-level numbers easier to compare.

Investors and rating agencies have begun to cross-check company disclosures against regulatory orders, satellite data and certificate registries, rather than relying on sustainability reports alone.

Analysts caution that headline sustainability claims are best read alongside the filed numbers, since the choice of baseline year and the use of intensity rather than absolute figures can change the picture considerably.

body:

headline: 5 forest-loss alerts recorded near Palar Rolling site in FY2024-25
body:

The disclosure carried reasonable assurance from Malhotra Bedi & Co.

Palar Rolling Mills Ltd is a steel and metals company headquartered in Kolkata, West Bengal. It reported turnover of Rs 18,667 crore in FY2023-24 and operates 4 facilities across Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Odisha and West Bengal. Its shares trade under the listing NSE: PALARSTL.

headline: NGT orders Arjuna Renewable to pay Rs 4.26 crore over fly ash lapses
body:
CHENNAI: The National Green Tribunal's Southern Zone bench at Chennai has directed Arjuna Renewable Power Ltd to pay a penalty of Rs 4.26 crore for fly ash utilisation below the prescribed norm and a breach of the ash dyke at its Chennai Thermal Power Station in Chennai, Tamil Nadu, according to an order dated 17 December 2024. The matter was registered as O.A. No. 213/2024 (SZ).

In its order, the bench applied the polluter pays principle and asked the Tamil Nadu Pollution Control Board to monitor compliance and report back to the tribunal. The tribunal said that the amount is meant to restore the environment and is not a substitute for any prosecution that the board may initiate under the Water and Air Acts.

body:

headline: Pharmaceuticals sector: regulators' orders in FY2024-25 add up to Rs 3.81 crore
body:
A review of regulatory records for FY2024-25 shows that companies in the pharmaceuticals sector were subject to 4 environmental orders, with total monetary penalties and compensation of Rs 3.81 crore.

The most significant orders were against Karna Formulations Ltd (NGT, 19 September 2024, environmental compensation, Rs 3.65 crore), Sabri Laboratories Ltd (NGT, 19 April 2024, environmental compensation, Rs 8 lakh), Konark API Industries Ltd (NGT, 11 November 2024, environmental compensation, Rs 8 lakh) and Cheyyar Lifesciences Ltd (GPCB, 1 January 2025, show cause).

By authority, the orders were split as follows: 3 from NGT and 1 from state boards. By type: 3 environmental compensation and 1 show cause.

Lawyers said that the mix of orders has shifted from simple show-cause notices towards compensation, in line with the polluter pays principle that the tribunal applies. They added that many orders are appealed and that the final amounts can differ from those initially directed.

Industry bodies said that the sector has been investing in pollution control and online monitoring, and that continuous data now makes violations easier to detect and verify. Several companies named above said that they had filed replies or paid under protest, and that they were reviewing their compliance systems.

Analysts said that the financial impact of individual orders is usually small relative to the turnover of the companies involved, but that repeated orders at the same site can lead to consent conditions that constrain production, which is the larger risk to earnings.

Companies in heavy industry have been asked by lenders and customers to disclose facility-level data, and many have started to publish site-wise emissions and water use alongside their annual reports.

Environmental lawyers said that the quality of data is now a bigger issue than its availability, since regulators, investors and communities increasingly compare several sources before forming a view on a company.

Industry associations said that compliance costs have risen across sectors, but argued that predictable rules and clear timelines are more important to investment decisions than the level of any single norm.
